newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian Grain-Market slide finally halts.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian Grain-Market slide finally halts.

text.p: Australia's protracted grain price slide seemed to finally turn toward the end of last week as futures prices rose, cash prices gained and further cuts in the Australian Wheat Board's (AWB) pool prices appeared unlikely.
Relief spread among futures brokers as buyers and sellers returned to the market.
Thoughts in the bush and in grain handling channels, however, turned to the extent of a likely downgrading of Australia's big wheat crop with forecast rain falling as the harvest got into stride.
"I hope (so)," said Cameron Pratt of GrainCorp when asked if the market had turned. "There seems to be a bit of support."
Since the A$15.00 a tonne price cut in the AWB's pool price to A$175.00 for Australian Standard White (ASW) on Monday night, futures prices levelled out supportively, he said.
With the 80 percent up-front pool payment guaranteed by the AWB, "it's (the pool price) probably about as low as it's going to go until the pool shuts," Pratt said.
But the stockfeed sector continued to hold back from the market, waiting for a downgrade of the crop, he said.
"With all this weather coming through there's sure to be some sort of downgrading eventually," he said.
Peter Howard of New England Agricultural Traders also has a crop downgrade in sight.
The harvest had not properly begun in the south of the eastern states and some rain was already falling in parts of the New South Wales grainbelt, he said.
"Certainly we would expect some downgrading (to have occurred) already," he said.

Pratt saw cash wheat prices up by about A$5.00 a tonne for ASW Newcastle over the past week. On Friday Newcastle bids were at about A$145 but sales did not occur with sellers looking for at least A$148 to A$150, he said.
"Everything's seems to have levelled off, if not even a tad higher as the harvest progressed," Howard said. "It may be a sign things have stabilised on our domestic market," he said.
Over the past week, AWB indicator prices in the main centres for ASW were steady to up by A$4.00 a tonne.
The turning point on the Sydney Futures Exchange came on Tuesday, when a record 261 trades went through including trades on the overnight SYCOM system the night before.
Wheat futures fell heavily on SYCOM Monday night after the pool price cut, with January 1997 down A$8.50 to A$138.00.

Prices fell on the SFE floor on Tuesday compared with floor closing prices on Monday, but were up from their overnight SYCOM lows. January 1997 closed at A$144.50 on Tuesday's floor trading, down by A$2.00 compared with Monday's floor close but up by A$6.50 on the SYCOM close overnight.
Slight falls on Wednesday also showed strength as SFE prices held out against a heavy overnight fall in Chicago.
On Thursday and Friday SFE prices clearly rose, with January 1997 up by A$2.00 on Thursday. Other contracts continued the rise on Friday, with May 1997 up by A$1.50 a tonne.
After Friday's close, Gary Booth of Ord Minnett Jardine Fleming Futures Ltd said the market was at or approaching its short-term bottom and was generally recognised as over-sold.
